This is a set of five disjointed letters, pronounced by the name of the letter and not by its named referent (musammā), because a letter has a name (ism) and a referent (musammā). For example, the word (كتب) has as its referent the word (kataba), but by its name it is (kāf, tā', bā'). So the name (ism) is the designation placed upon the utterance.

In the Noble Qur'an there are many surahs that begin with disjointed letters, pronounced by the name of the letter and not its referent. These letters may be a single letter, such as: Nūn, Ṣād, Qāf. They may be two letters, such as: Ṭā Hā, Ṭā Sīn. They may be three letters, such as: Alif Lām Mīm, Ṭā Sīn Mīm. They may come as four letters, such as: Alif Lām Mīm Rā. And they may come as five letters, such as: Kāf Hā' Yā' 'Ayn Ṣād, Ḥā' Mīm 'Ayn Sīn Qāf.

Therefore we say: learning the Qur'an necessarily requires oral transmission (samā'), for otherwise how would you distinguish between Alif Lām Mīm at the beginning of al-Baqara, which you pronounce separated, and the verse ﴿Did We not expand for you your breast?﴾ (Surah al-Sharh) which you pronounce joined? And God the Exalted spoke the truth when He said: ﴿So when We have recited it, then follow its recitation.﴾ (Surah al-Qiyamah).

We observe regarding these letters that the referent is pronounced by the learner and the non-learner alike, whereas the name is not pronounced except by the learner who knows the letters of the alphabet. So if the Messenger of God (ﷺ) was unlettered (ummī), who did not sit with a teacher, and this is by the testimony of his enemies, then who taught him these letters?

Thus, when you see these disjointed letters, know that God, glorified and exalted, pronounced them by the names of the letters, while we speak by the referents of the letters, not by their names.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1–53, fragments of 54–66) on surah 19, verse 2:

Al-dhikr (remembrance, mention): it has several meanings. Al-dhikr is the giving of news about a thing at the outset, and speaking about something of which you had no prior knowledge; and it is also a reminder of something you had known before, which we wish to remind you of, as in His saying, ﴿And remind, for indeed the reminder benefits the believers﴾ (Surat al-Dhariyat: 55).

Al-dhikr is also applied to the Qur'an: ﴿Indeed, We have sent down the Reminder, and indeed We will be its guardian﴾ (Surat al-Hijr: 9).

In the Qur'an is the best of remembrance and the truest of reports and events. Al-dhikr is also applied to every earlier book from Allah, as in His saying: ﴿So ask the people of the Reminder if you do not know﴾ (Surat al-Nahl: 43).

Al-dhikr is also fame, elevation and honour, as in His saying: ﴿And indeed it is a Reminder for you and your people…﴾ (Surat al-Zukhruf: 44).

And His saying: ﴿Indeed We have sent down to you a Book in which is your Reminder…﴾ (Surat al-Anbiya': 10), meaning: in it is your fame and your honour. From this is our saying: "So-and-so has a reputation (dhikr) among his people." Among al-dhikr is also a human's remembrance of his Lord through obedience and worship, and the Lord's remembrance of His servant through reward, recompense and mercy. From this is His saying: ﴿So remember Me, I will remember you…﴾ (Surat al-Baqarah: 152).

From His saying: ﴿A mention of the mercy of your Lord…﴾ (Surah Maryam: 2), meaning: this, O Muhammad, is the news of Zakariyya, his story, and Allah's mercy upon him.

Al-rahmah (mercy) is the manifestation of the Merciful upon the one shown mercy, by which his righteousness for his task is made to endure. Thus every merciful one, even among humans, and every one shown mercy, even among humans — what does he do? He gives another some advice that helps him to carry out his task in the most complete manner. So what of it if the mercy of Allah is for the best of His creation, Muhammad?

It is a general mercy and an all-encompassing mercy, because he (ﷺ) is the noblest of the prophets, the most honourable of them, and their seal; there is no revelation or message after him, nor any completion. Thus he is the noblest of creation, and the mercy of every prophet takes its share from the Truth, glory be to Him, according to the measure of his task, and the task of Muhammad is the most noble of tasks.

The word "mercy" (rahmah) here is a verbal noun (masdar) that conveys the meaning of its verb. The verbal noun, like the verb, requires a subject and an object, as we say: "The beating of the man of his son pained me" (ālamanī ḍarb al-rajul waladahu). So the meaning of ﴿Raḥmatu rabbika ʿabdahu Zakariyya﴾ (Surah Maryam: 2) is: your Lord showed mercy to His servant Zakariyya. Therefore He said, ﴿Mention of the mercy of your Lord…﴾ (Surah Maryam: 2), because it is the highest kind of mercy. And although here He mentions His mercy toward His servant Zakariyya, He addressed Muhammad (ﷺ) with His saying: ﴿And We have not sent you except as a mercy to the worlds﴾ (Surat al-Anbiya': 107).

So Allah's mercy toward Muhammad is not a mercy specific to him; rather it is a general mercy for all who act, and this is a great and lofty station. Thus what is meant by ﴿Mention of the mercy of your Lord to His servant Zakariyya﴾ (Surah Maryam: 2)...

That is: what is recited to you now, O Muhammad, is the mention, narrative and report of the mercy of your Lord, which is the most excellent of mercies, upon His servant Zakariyya. We have already explained that servitude to creation is humiliation and debasement, a hideous word that is unacceptable; whereas servitude to Allah, exalted is He, is might and honour, indeed the utmost of might, honour and dignity. We explained this by saying that the servitude that brings harm and sorrow is the servitude of a slave to a master who takes his goodness, whereas in servitude to Allah the servant takes the goodness of his Master.

But what kind of mercy did Allah, exalted is He, manifest when He informed His Messenger (ﷺ) of the news of His servant Zakariyya?

They said: it is a mercy connected with the absoluteness of power in the universe, and the absoluteness of power in that Allah, blessed and exalted is He, created causes for effects, then said to the causes: "You are not acting by your own essence, but by My will and My power. If I wish that you not act, I nullify your action; and if you cannot rise to good by yourself, I make you rise to it."

Among that is what happened in the story of the Friend of Allah, Ibrahim, when the disbelievers threw him into the fire. It was not Allah's purpose, in extinguishing the fire for Ibrahim, or in making the fire coolness and safety for Ibrahim, to save Ibrahim; for it was possible that He could have prevented the opponents of Ibrahim, peace be upon him, from seizing him, or sent down rain to extinguish the fire they had kindled. But the spite of the people does not lie in this: had Ibrahim escaped their grip, or had rain fallen and extinguished the fire, they would have said, "Had we gained power over him, we would have done such and such to him, and had the rain not fallen, we would have done such and such to him."

So: the will of Allah willed to outwit these people, and to show them the absoluteness of divine power by enabling them to seize Ibrahim until they actually threw him into the fire; then came the supreme command from the Creator, glory be to Him, to the fire that its property of burning be nullified:

﴿We said: O fire, be coolness and safety upon Ibrahim﴾ (Surat al-Anbiya': 69).

Likewise, in the story of Allah's mercy toward His servant Zakariyya, it gives us evidence of the absoluteness of power in the matter of creation, and it draws our attention to the fact that the Creator, glory be to Him and exalted is He, made causes for the universe; for the Creator, glory be to Him, may give you through causes, and may cancel them entirely and bring about effects without causes.

The absoluteness of power also appeared in the story of the beginning of creation. We know that the multiplication and proliferation of people occurs through the union of a man and a woman; yet the absoluteness of power is not confined to these causes, and the Creator, glory be to Him, manages His creation in every mode of creation: Adam came without male or female, He created Eve from a male without a female, and He created Jesus from a female without a male.

Thus divine power is not restricted by causes, and this absoluteness of power in creation continues until the Hour arises: we see a man and a woman as spouses, but no procreation takes place between them, and their causes are rendered inoperative, lest we rely on causes and forget the Causer, glory be to Him. He is the One who said:

﴿To Allah belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth; He creates what He wills; He bestows female [offspring] on whom He wills, and bestows male [offspring] on whom He wills, or He pairs them, males and females, and He makes whom He wills barren; indeed He is All-Knowing, All-Powerful﴾ (Surat al-Shura: 49–50).

The absoluteness of power in the story of Zakariyya, peace be upon him, is manifest in that Allah, exalted is He, responded to Zakariyya's supplication that He grant him a child. Allah said: ﴿A mention of the mercy of your Lord to His servant Zakariyya﴾ (Surah Maryam: 2), meaning: Allah showed him mercy. But when was this mercy?

Meaning: at the time when he called upon his Lord with a secret call.

Calling (nida') is one of the forms of speech (asalib kalamiyya). The rhetoricians divide speech into informative (khabar) and inshai (insha'), and calling belongs to the latter, which is a request for something from the addressee. If you say "O Muhammad," you intend to bring about his attention and turning toward you. So calling means seeking that the other turn toward you. But can calling from God, Exalted is He, carry this meaning? You only call someone who is distant from you, whom you want to bring near to you.

How, then, do you call your Lord, blessed and exalted, when He is nearer to you than your jugular vein? And how do you call Him, glorified is He, when He hears you even before you speak? If His turning toward you exists at all times, what is the purpose of calling here?

We say: the purpose of calling is supplication (du'a'). The description of the call here as ﴿a secret call﴾ [Maryam 19:3] is because it is not like the calling of creatures to creatures, which requires raising the voice so that it may be heard. It is a call to Allah, blessed and exalted, for whom secret and open speech are equal, and He says:

﴿And keep your speech secret or declare it; indeed, He is Knower of what is within the breasts﴾ [al-Mulk 67:13].

And from the etiquette of supplication is that we call upon Him, glorified is He, as He has commanded us:

﴿Call upon your Lord humbly and in secret...﴾ [al-A'raf 7:55].

And He, glorified is He, says: ﴿He knows the secret and what is more hidden﴾ [Ta-Ha 20:7], meaning: and what is more hidden than the secret; for He, glorified is He, knew before a thing became secret that it would become secret. Therefore, the Truth, glorified is He, made the best supplication the hidden supplication, because a person may ask his Lord for something which, if others hear, they may belittle him for it, so the supplication was made hidden between the servant and his Lord so that his affair is not exposed before people.

As for the Truth, glorified is He, He is a Veiler who loves concealment, even over the disobedient. Likewise, the servant calls upon his Lord with what he would be shy to mention before people, and so that he may be free in supplication, asking his Lord for whatever he wills, because He is his Lord and his Protector to whom he turns for refuge. If people grow sorrowful and impatient when you ask them for the least thing, Allah, Exalted, rejoices in you when you ask Him.

But why did Zakariyya conceal his supplication?

Zakariyya supplicated his Lord to grant him a child, but how could this request be fulfilled when he had reached great old age and his wife was barren? It was as though all the causes present were inoperative for him. Therefore he turned to Allah with supplication: "O Lord, I have no refuge but You. You alone are capable of breaking the law and the established order." This was a request from Zakariyya that came at an unusual time.

He also concealed it because he sought a child while his paternal cousins were present, who would carry his methodology after him. Yet he did not entrust them with the methodology of Allah, because the outward conduct of their lives was not consistent with that methodology. How could he entrust them with the methodology of Allah when they were not trustworthy over their own selves? So if Zakariyya asked his Lord to grant him a child to inherit prophethood after him, these people would be angered by Zakariyya's supplication and would oppose him. Therefore his supplication came hidden, secret between him and his Lord, Exalted is He. Zakariyya, peace be upon him, explained the reason for this in the following verses when he said: ﴿who will inherit from me and inherit from the family of Ya'qub...﴾ [Maryam 19:6].

So, the reason for seeking a child is purely religious; it is not sought for worldly gain. His eagerness for a child was only that he did not feel safe that the people after him would preserve the methodology of Allah and protect it from corruption.

Therefore his saying ﴿who will inherit from me﴾ here is not to be understood as inheritance of wealth, as some imagine, since prophets do not bequeath inheritance, as the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said: "We, the company of prophets, do not leave inheritance; what we leave is charity."

Thus the Prophet departs this world without any of his relatives benefiting from his wealth, even the poor among them. The matter with the prophets is entirely sincere for the sake of Allah, Exalted is He. Therefore He said after it: ﴿and inherit from the family of Ya'qub...﴾ [Maryam 19:6], meaning: the prophethood which they transmitted among themselves. It is therefore by no means correct to understand the inheritance here as inheritance of wealth or the transient goods of this world. Among the same usage is His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And Sulayman inherited from Dawud...﴾ [al-Naml 27:16]. In what did he inherit from him? In prophethood and kingship. The matter is far removed from material inheritance.

This is the call, or the supplication, with which Zakariyya (peace be upon him) called upon his Lord: ﴿My Lord, indeed my bones have weakened, and my head has blazed with grey hair.﴾ (Surah Maryam)

In supplication, it is recommended to say: "Yā Rabb" (O Lord).

Or one may say: "Yā Allāh." Zakariyya said "Rabb" (Lord), meaning "Yā Rabb," because he was asking for something connected with the bestowal of lordship (ʿaṭāʾ al-rubūbiyyah), which encompasses both the believer and the disbeliever. He was asking for a child, and this is a matter connected with the structure of life and its fitness for procreation, and it is among the gifts of the Lord, glory be to Him, after the father's [ability].

It is as if Zakariyya (peace be upon him) said to his Lord: "O Lord, O You who give to the one who believes in You and give to the one who disbelieves; O You who give to the one who obeys and give to the one who disobeys. Far be it from You to withhold Your bounty from one who obeys You and calls people to Your obedience."

As for supplication with "Allāh," it concerns matters of worship and obligation.

Then Zakariyya (peace be upon him) presents the grounds (ḥaythiyyāt) of this request: ﴿My Lord, indeed my bones have weakened...﴾ (Surah Maryam). "Wahn" is weakness. He said "al-ʿaẓm" (the bones) because everything has a form of firmness and strength: water, for example, has a known consistency; fat has a consistency; flesh has a consistency; sinew and bone, and all the elements of human composition. The bone is the strongest of these things, and in the structure of the human body the bone is like the "chassis" in modern terminology. On the bone the human body is built of flesh, blood and sinew. So if the bones, which are the strongest elements, become weak, then the rest is weaker still, a fortiori.

Therefore, when the Arab complained of drought and famine, what did he say?

He said: "Difficult years have passed over us. A year melted the fat," that is, after hunger and the absence of food; "a year took away the flesh," that is, after it had finished off the fat; "and a year wiped out the bone."

It is as if the bone is the last storehouse of sustenance in the human body at the moment when food and drink are cut off from it. In this state the bone directs its nourishment especially to the brain, because as long as there remains in the brain a capacity to accept life, whatever damage has befallen the body is repairable and can return to its normal state. Thus, the human being's well-being is tied to the well-being of the brain.

Accordingly, we find that physicians in critical cases focus their attention on the well-being of the brain, and upon it they base the life or death of the person. Even if the heart stops, they can by massage restore it to its normal state; but if the brain stops, this means death.

It is as if the Prophet of God, Zakariyya (peace be upon him), says: "O Lord, my bone has weakened, and I have no remaining source except the last resource for preserving life."

Since the bone is something inward, buried beneath the skin, it is an inward ground, so Zakariyya (peace be upon him) wished to bring another ground that is outward and manifest, and he brought a clear matter: ﴿and the head has blazed with grey hair﴾ (Maryam). He likened the spread of white hair on his head to the kindling of fire; the white hair covering it is as conspicuous as fire.

Whoever reflects on this simile finds that fire too feeds on firewood and remains kindled, having a flame that rises as long as there is in the wood the vegetative vitality that feeds the fire. When this vegetative vitality in the wood ends, the fire begins to diminish until it becomes an ember without flame, and then it goes out.

The kindling of the head with fire is also a sign of the weakening of the body and the feebleness of its strength, because hair acquires its colour from a pigmented substance, black, red or yellow, found in the hair bulb, which supplies the hair with this colour. The weakness of the body gradually weakens this substance until it disappears, and consequently the hair emerges white. Whiteness is not a colour; rather, whiteness is the absence of colour, the result of the body's weakness and the weakening of the glands that secrete this colour.

Therefore, we find that the affluent, who take great care of their hair and apply various substances to it, first see whitening at their temples (sawālif), because the temples, after the barber has trimmed them, absorb the greatest quantity of caustic substances that affect the hair follicles and this pigment. The hair is like a tube; these substances easily penetrate it, especially directly after shaving, while the hair is still open.

Then he says: ﴿and I have never been, in my supplication to You, my Lord, unblessed﴾ (Maryam). That is: I have never, in the past, been wretched because of my supplication to You, since I was answered by You; as You honoured me previously with an answer, I was never wretched through my supplication but rather happy with the answer. So do not break Your custom with me this time, and make me happy by answering me, especially since my request of You is an act of obedience to You. I do not wish to leave this world except while I am at peace concerning the one who will carry this method and perform this task after me.

You may call upon God for a matter you love, and if what you love does not come, or you are not answered, you grieve as if you had become wretched through your supplication. Your wretchedness may be an illusion, because you do not know the wisdom in non-answer; you do not know that God, exalted is He, controls your affairs.

Perhaps you supplicate for something you see as good from your own viewpoint, while in God's knowledge there is no good for you in it; so He withholds it from you and corrects for you what you erred in estimating as good. Your Lord gives you from where you think He has withheld from you, and does good to you from where you think He has deprived you, because you sought good from where you know it to be good, and God withholds from where He knows that good is not in that.

Then Zakariyya (peace be upon him) mentions another reason, which is the reason behind all reasons and the core of this matter.

(Al-mawali) comes from al-wala', and they are his relatives, the sons of his paternal uncles. They are the second generation that will come after him, and he fears that they will carry the method and the religion of God after him, because he has seen in their conduct in life that they are not fit to bear this task. ﴿from behind me..." 5 "﴾ (Surat Maryam).

We have already explained in Surat al-Kahf that the word wara' comes with the meanings: behind, in front of, after, or other than. Here it has the meaning: after me. Then he says: ﴿and my wife is barren..." 5 "﴾ (Surat Maryam).

The 'aqir (barren woman) is one who does not bear children by her nature from the beginning, or who has become barren because she has reached the age of menopause, for example. We know that reproduction and procreation in the human species arise from a man and a woman. Zakariyya has already described his own state of weakness and old age, and then he reports that his wife is barren and does not bear children. So all the causes of having children are rendered inoperative.

His saying ﴿and my wife is barren..." 5 "﴾ (Surat Maryam) means: she is barren by her very nature, and this is a condition accompanying her, not something that befell her; it had not happened to her before.

Then he says ﴿so grant me..." 5 "﴾ (Surat Maryam). Hibah (gift) is giving without a return. Here the causes are inoperative, and the premises say: there is no procreation. Therefore he did not say, for example, "give me," because giving may be in exchange for something. In this case, however, the giving is without an exchange and without premises. It is as if he said: "O Lord, if You are going to give me a child, it is a gift from You, whose causes I do not possess." For this reason He said in another verse about Ibrahim (peace be upon him):

﴿Praise be to God who has granted me, in old age, Isma'il..." 39 "﴾ (Surat Ibrahim).

We have a pause and an observation on His saying ﴿in old age..." 39 "﴾ (Surat Ibrahim).

The exegetes said that ('ala) here means (ma'a, "with"). ('ala) has three letters and (ma'a) has two letters, so why did the Truth, blessed and exalted, shift from the lighter to the heavier? There must be an additional nuance behind this wording: ma'a indicates only accompaniment, whereas 'ala indicates both accompaniment and elevation. It is as if he said: "Indeed, old age, O Lord, requires that a child not exist, but Your absolute power is higher than old age." Similarly His saying:

﴿And indeed your Lord is full of forgiveness for mankind despite their wrongdoing..." 6 "﴾ (Surat al-Ra'd). As if wrongdoing requires that they be punished, but God's mercy toward them and His forgiveness of them rose above the deserved punishment.

His saying ﴿from Yourself..." 5 "﴾ (Surat Maryam) means: from Your own presence, not through causes, ﴿a protector (waliyy)..." 5 "﴾, that is, a righteous son who will succeed me in bearing the trust of conveying Your method to people, so that the movement of life may be sound for them.

Earlier we clarified that inheritance here does not mean inheritance of wealth, because the prophets do not bequeath; whatever wealth they leave behind is charity after them. What is meant here is the inheritance of knowledge, prophethood, and rulership, and the carrying of God's method to people. We note that he did not suffice with saying (yarithuni) but said (wa-yarith min Al Ya'qub). For I am not the summit of obedience within the family of Ya'qub: there are Ibrahim, Isma'il, Ishaq and Ya'qub. This is humility on his part, and consideration for the ranks of men and placing them in their proper stations. And his saying: ﴿Make him, my Lord, one with whom You are pleased﴾ (Surat Maryam, 19:6).

Meaning: well-pleasing to You.

**Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 19, verse 7:**

The one who reflects on this story finds that this verse has omitted from the narrative whatever its context makes understood, trusting the listener's perceptiveness and his ability to complete the meaning. So the sense of the verse is: God heard Zakariya's supplication and the circumstances of his request, and answered him with His words: ﴿O Zakariya, (7)﴾ [Maryam 19:7]. Addressing Zakariya (peace be upon him) directly in this way is evidence of the swiftness of the response to his supplication, so the answer came immediately, without preliminaries.

An example of this is what the Qur'an relates of the story of Sulayman (peace be upon him) and Bilqis. Sulayman said:

﴿O assembly, which of you will bring me her throne before they come to me in submission? (38)﴾ A stronger one among the jinn said: ﴿I will bring it to you before you rise from your place; indeed, I am strong and trustworthy for it. (39)﴾ One who had knowledge of the Scripture said: ﴿I will bring it to you before your glance returns to you.﴾ Then when he saw it placed beside him, he said: ﴿This is from the bounty of my Lord to test me whether I will be grateful or ungrateful. And whoever is grateful, his gratitude is only for himself; and whoever is ungrateful, indeed my Lord is Free of need and Generous. (40)﴾ (Surat al-Naml)

Between His words ﴿before your glance returns to you (40)﴾ and ﴿he saw it placed beside him (40)﴾ lies a statement that the context of the story requires, as if we were to say: "He gave him permission, so he went and brought the throne." But the wording comes swiftly, to match the speed of the event of bringing Bilqis's throne from its place.

As for His words ﴿We give you good news (7)﴾ [Maryam 19:7]: bushra (glad tidings) is the announcement of something that will please you before it arrives, in order to prolong the joy of the pleasing thing. A person may bring you good news who is in fact deceitful, and events and circumstances may turn out contrary to what one expects. So how about when Allah the Exalted gives you good news? At the moment the glad tidings come from Allah, know that they are true and real, with no doubt in them.

His words ﴿a boy whose name is Yahya (7)﴾ [Maryam 19:7] mean: and He named him as well. We know that people have choices in giving names to what is named, and they have freedom in this. One woman names her son Harankash, and he is free; another names her black daughter Qamar, and she too is free.

However, when people name, they hope that the named will possess qualities that please the soul and gladden the eye. When you name someone "Sa'id" (happy), out of optimism that he will in fact be happy, the name is set to indicate the one named. But can this optimistic person bring about that the named will be as he loves and wishes? No, he possesses no such power and cannot guarantee it, because there is a higher power than him that governs this matter, and the named may turn out other than he intended.

As for when the one who names is Allah the Exalted, the name must come true in the one named and apply to him, and His intention for the one He names must be fulfilled. Allah, blessed and exalted, named the son of Zakariya Yahya, so this attribute must apply to him. Yahya is the opposite of one who dies. Thus He, glorified be He, is able to keep him alive, but for how long, and how many years? Life and living are realized here even if only through the average lifespan, for example. He gave him life, and the attribute of life was realized in him.

For this reason, the people of gnosis (ahl al-ma'rifa) inferred from his being named Yahya that the son of Zakariya would die as a martyr, so that he would remain alive as Allah named him, and so it was.

His words ﴿We had not made for him any namesake before (7)﴾ [Maryam 19:7]:

As for al-samiyy (namesake), the scholars differed about its meaning. They said it comes to mean: an equal, a peer, or a likeness; and as for "samiyyan," it means: one with the same name as him. An example is His saying, exalted be He:

﴿Lord of the heavens and the earth and whatever is between them, so worship Him and be steadfast in His worship. Do you know of anyone with His name? (65)﴾ [Maryam 19:65]

They said that samiyyan here carries both meanings: "Do you know anyone equal to Him or like Him?" because He, glorified and exalted be He, is ﴿There is nothing like Him (11)﴾ [al-Shura 42:11], and ﴿And there is none comparable to Him (4)﴾ [al-Ikhlas 112:4]. It is possible to take this meaning also in the story of Yahya (peace be upon him), except that a problem arises in it. When Allah, the Exalted, said regarding Yahya: ﴿We had not made for him any namesake before (7)﴾, and we take it to mean an equal, a peer, or a likeness, this would mean that no one like Yahya in righteousness and piety came before him. Then where is the father of the prophets, Ibrahim (peace be upon him)? And where are Isma'il and Ishaq?

So this meaning, although the context may allow it in other matters, does not fit here, because Allah had made before Yahya someone better than Yahya or at least like him. The other meaning, then, is: ﴿Do you know of anyone with His name? (65)﴾, that is, is there anyone named by His name, exalted be He? This is the meaning that fits the story of Yahya (peace be upon him), because he was the first name that the Real, glorified be He, placed on the son of Zakariya, and no one had been named by it before. After him, however, this name spread, until the poet said:

*I named him Yahya, that Yahya might live, but there was no way to repel the decree of God concerning him.*

Here we pause at one of the signs of Allah in naming: no disbelieving atheist, who openly declares his unbelief and proclaims his denial of the Creator, glorified be He, has dared to name his son "Allah." Yet freedom in choosing names is guaranteed. If this proves anything, it proves that their disbelief is stubborn obstinacy and that they are not sincere in their disbelief; they know that Allah exists, and therefore they fear for themselves and for their children to be named by this name.

So the word (samiyyan) in the matter of divinity is taken in both meanings, whereas in the matter of Yahya it admits only the second meaning.

Suppose that the Real, glorified and exalted be He, reviewed the names of the past and found that no one in the past had been named "Allah," so He declared it as a challenge: ﴿Do you know of anyone with His name? (65)﴾. After this challenge, no one dares to be named by this name.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 19, verse 8:

When Zakariyya, peace be upon him, heard the good news from his Lord, and was reassured that it would come to pass, this prompted him to delve into knowing the means, and how this would be accomplished, and how this glad tidings would be realized, given that he had reached extreme old age (﴿ataa*), and his wife was barren?

But what did Zakariyya intend by his question, when he knew well that God Most High had knowledge of his state and the state of his wife? The reality is that Zakariyya, peace be upon him, did not deny the occurrence of this glad tidings, and did not challenge God, far be it from him to intend that. Rather, the good news made him eager to know the manner of it, as happened in the story of Musa, peace be upon him, when his Lord spoke to him, chose him, and singled him out with this distinction, so speech led him to ask for the vision, and he said: ﴿My Lord, show me Yourself that I may look upon You.﴾ (Surat al-A'raf, 143). And as happened in the story of Ibrahim, peace be upon him, when he said to his Lord:

﴿My Lord, show me how You give life to the dead.﴾ (Surat al-Baqara, 260).

The father of the prophets did not doubt God's power to give life to the dead, but he wanted to know this wondrous method. The matter is not, in reality, one of existence or non-existence; it concerns the manner, and has nothing to do with existence.

So God, glorified be He, informed him that this matter is not to be merely spoken about, but must be carried out in practice. He commanded him, as we know from that story, to bring four birds himself, then to gather them to himself so that he could verify their reality for himself. Then He commanded him to cut them into pieces, then to scatter these pieces over the tops of the mountains. After that, the Creator, glorified be He, left it to him to call them himself, and for the command to come from him, so that these scattered pieces would gather together and life would return to them anew. This is one of the manifestations of His greatness, glorified and exalted be He: that He did not do it Himself, but made the one who could not do it able to do it and capable of it.

For if people consider the effect of their power to be on the weak, one who is unable to carry something brings someone to carry it for him, and he himself remains weak and unable to do anything. But God Most High extends His strength by Himself to the weak, so that he becomes strong and capable of acting. So His words ﴿How can I have a son?﴾ (Surat Maryam, 8) are a question about the manner, just as when Ibrahim, peace be upon him, was addressed by his Lord: ﴿Have you not believed?﴾ (Surat al-Baqara, 260), meaning: in My power to give life to the dead. He said: ﴿Yes⁠—﴾, meaning: yes, I believe. ﴿But that my heart may be assured⁠﴾ (Surat al-Baqara, 260), meaning: regarding the manner in which the giving of life is accomplished. Or: Zakariyya, peace be upon him, by his words ﴿How can I have a son?﴾ (Surat Maryam, 8), wants to confirm this glad tidings and record it, just as when you promise your child that you will buy him a gift, he persists in this matter to confirm your promise to him, and takes pleasure in it being a realized promise with no doubt in it. Then Zakariyya mentions the grounds for his wonder at this matter, saying: ﴿My wife is barren and I have reached extreme old age﴾ (Surat Maryam, 8). ʿitiyy (utter decrepitude), from ʿatā, means to transgress, to be arrogant, and to cause great corruption; and al-ʿutuww means disbelief, while al-ʿatiyy is the strong one who cannot be overcome. Therefore, old age, which is a symbol of weakness, was described as ʿatiyy, because the weakness of gray hair and senility is a weakness that no one can resist or repel, no matter how much one tries to counter it with medicines and drugs (and vitamins).

It seems that this matter of a child was preoccupying Zakariyya, peace be upon him, and pressing upon him, because he had called upon God often to grant him a child. In another place He says: ﴿My Lord, do not leave me alone, and You are the best of inheritors﴾ (Surat al-Anbiya, 89).

So Zakariyya, peace be upon him, wants a child who will inherit from him, and he is an heir, since God Most High is the best of inheritors. But the response comes:

﴿So We responded to him and gave him Yahya, and We made his wife fit for him.﴾ (Surat al-Anbiya, 90).

We note that God Most High mentioned first ﴿and We made his wife fit for him﴾ (Surat al-Anbiya, 90), who was going to bear this child, and then said ﴿and We gave him Yahya﴾ (Surat al-Anbiya, 90). So the fitness of the wife was not a condition for this glad tidings or for the occurrence of this gift.

Here is a manifestation of the comprehensive power of God, which nothing can overwhelm. He, glorified be He, is able to restore this barren wife to fitness, for the divine craftsmanship does not stop at any limit. It is like when one of your appliances breaks down, for example, and you take it to the electrician to repair it, and he finds the damage to be severe, and advises you to abandon it and buy a new one, because there is no way to fix it.

Therefore God Most High restored Zakariyya's wife, so that we would not suppose that Yahya came by some other means, and the wife remained in her condition.

(Al-Sha'rawi said, i.e., the Almighty and Exalted):

﴿"Thus said your Lord: 'It is easy for Me...'"﴾ (Surah Maryam, 19:9). That is, He, exalted is He, said this and decreed it, so do not dispute this matter. We know you better and know what you are in, namely old age, and that your wife is barren; nevertheless, I will bestow upon you a son.

His, exalted is He, saying: ﴿"It is easy for Me..."﴾ (Surah Maryam, 19:9).

In another verse, concerning the resurrection, He says: ﴿"And it is easier for Him..."﴾ (Surah al-Rum, 30:27). Do not think that, with respect to God, there is something easy, something easier, and something difficult, for the purpose of these expressions is to bring the meaning closer to our minds.

The Almighty addresses us in terms of our own speech and our own logic. Creating from something that exists is, in our view, easier than creating from something that does not exist, as the Almighty said:

﴿"Were We then wearied by the first creation? Nay, but they are in doubt about a new creation."﴾ (Surah Qaf, 50:15).

Thus, with respect to His bringing things into existence, there is no "easy" and "easier," or "hard" and "harder," because these terms are used for one who performs actions through treatment and practice, and this applies to our human works. As for the Blessed and Exalted, He does not treat actions; rather, He says to a thing "Be," and it is:

﴿"His command, when He intends a thing, is only that He says to it, 'Be,' and it is."﴾ (Surah Ya-Sin, 36:82).

Then the Almighty argues from the stronger case, saying:

﴿"And I had already created you before, when you were nothing."﴾ (Surah Maryam, 19:9).

So, for Yahya to come into existence from something is less strange than for me to bring into existence one who was nothing.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1–53, fragments of 54–66) on surah 19, verse 10:

(Ayah) That is: a sign that his wife has conceived Yahya. It is as though Zakariyya, peace be upon him, was hastening matters and had no patience for the nine months; he wanted to live in the shade of this blessing, as though it were a settled fact, his tongue never ceasing to praise and thank God for it, and the blessing remaining in his mind even though his son was still a fetus in his mother's womb.

So his Lord answers him: ﴿Your sign is that you will not speak to the people for three nights, while being sound.﴾ (Surat Maryam)

Your sign is that you will not speak to the people for three nights. The word "alla" (that... not) here is not a prohibition on speech; rather, it is an announcement of a condition that will befall him without his will, so that he will not speak to people while his limbs are sound and without any impediment preventing speech, such as muteness or otherwise. Therefore He said: ﴿for three nights, while being sound.﴾ (Surat Maryam), that is: healthy and whole, sound in creation, with no deficiency in you and no defect in any of your limbs. Thus the inability to speak is not a defect, but a sign from the signs of God. There is a difference between a cosmic (kawni) matter and a legislative (shar'i) matter. The cosmic matter is that which happens, and you have no choice in preventing it; the legislative matter is that in which you have a choice, so that you may obey it and become obedient, or disobey it and become disobedient.

What happened to Zakariyya was a cosmic matter, a sign from God in which he had no choice. It is as though the Exalted One is giving us the evidence that there exists that which is not bound by apparent causes: the causes may remain sound and suitable while the effect does not appear. The tongue here is present, the organs of speech are sound, yet he is unable to speak.

Reflect, then, on the perfect freedom of power: God willed for Zakariyya a child without (apparent) causes, and here He withheld speech in the presence of the causes. Both signs are equal in His power and His will, exalted is He.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 19, verse 11:

So this matter befell Zakariyya while he was in the (mihrab), that is, the place of worship and prayer. It is usually elevated, raised above what surrounds it, and it was the prayer place of the prophets and the righteous. It was called mihrab (a place of struggle) because the Shaytan is fought off in it by his schemes and whisperings. The mihrab is also mentioned in the story of Dawud, peace be upon him:

﴿Then the angels called to him while he stood praying in the mihrab: "Allah gives you good news of Yahya, confirming a word from Allah..."﴾ (Surat Al 'Imran) [3:39]

And His saying, exalted is He:

﴿So he [Zakariyya] signalled to them...﴾ (Surat Maryam) [19:11]

We have said that wahy (revelation) has a linguistic meaning and a legal meaning. Wahy linguistically is informing by a hidden way. On this meaning it comes in many ways: Allah, exalted is He, reveals to the messengers and prophets, and He reveals to non-messengers among the chosen, as in His saying, exalted is He:

﴿And We revealed to the mother of Musa, "Suckle him..."﴾ (Surat Al-Qasas) [28:7], that is, He informed her by a hidden way, which is the way of inspiration (ilham). He reveals to the angels:

﴿When your Lord revealed to the angels, "I am with you, so strengthen those who believe..."﴾ (Surat Al-Anfal) [8:12]

He reveals to the righteous among the followers of the messengers:

﴿And when I revealed to the disciples, "Believe in Me and in My messenger..."﴾ (Surat Al-Ma'idah) [5:111]

Wahy extends by hidden indication to insects:

﴿And your Lord revealed to the bee, "Take for yourself houses in the mountains and in the trees and in what they construct..."﴾ (Surat An-Nahl) [16:68]

Indeed, wahy extends to inanimate matter in His saying:

﴿When the earth is shaken with its [final] shaking, and the earth brings forth its burdens, and man says, "What is wrong with it?" On that Day it will report its news, because your Lord has revealed to it.﴾ (Surat Az-Zalzalah) [99:1-5]

And the devils sometimes reveal to one another:

﴿They inspire one another with decorated speech as deception...﴾ (Surat Al-An'am) [6:112]

And they reveal to their allies:

﴿And indeed, the devils inspire to their allies to dispute with you...﴾ (Surat Al-An'am) [6:121]

As for legal wahy, it is the informing from Allah alone to a prophet who claims prophethood and who has with him a miracle (mu'jizah). So wahy is: hidden informing from Allah to the messenger. His saying, exalted is He:

﴿So he signalled to them...﴾ (Surat Maryam) [19:11], that is, he told them by way of gesture, because he could not speak, ﴿to glorify [Allah] morning and evening﴾ (Surat Maryam) [19:11].

Bukrah (morning) is the beginning of the day, and 'ashiyy (evening) is its end, meaning: encircle the day with glorification at its beginning and its end. It seems that Zakariyya, peace be upon him, showed signs of joy and elation at the glad tidings, and he saw that his thanks to Allah and his glorification were not adequate for this blessing, so he commanded his people to glorify Allah along with him and to thank Him with him for this blessing, because it does not belong to him alone but is general to the whole people.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1–53, fragments of 54–66) on surah 19, verse 12:

We notice that the noble verse has carried us over a wide stretch and passed over a long period of the life of Yahya, peace be upon him. The context had been speaking of him as good news for his father while he was still a foetus in his mother's womb, and suddenly it addresses him as though he had already become a settled fact: ﴿O Yahya, take the Book with strength.﴾ [19:12] He had reached the stage of maturity and become fit to bear the mission of da'wah (calling to God). So the matter is treated in earnest, and it is an actual reality. His saying ﴿take the Book﴾ means the Torah, which contains God's method that organises their life's movement. ﴿With strength﴾ means with sincerity in memorising it and eagerness to act upon it, because the heavenly knowledge and divine method that came to you in the Torah is not meant merely for you to know it, but also to act upon it. Otherwise, God Most High has said concerning the Children of Israel: ﴿The likeness of those who were entrusted with the Torah and then did not bear it is like the donkey that carries books. Evil is the likeness of the people who deny the signs of God.﴾ [62:5] God entrusted them with the Torah, but they did not bear it and did not act upon it.

Strength (quwwah) is the active energy that turns the wheel of life, in motion and in stillness. Take as an example a spacecraft that launches into outer space and keeps circulating in it for several years, and you wonder: where does it get the fuel that moves it throughout this period? The truth is that it needs fuel only in the amount that lifts it out of the orbit of Earth's gravity. Once it leaves the sphere of gravity while moving, it remains moving and does not stop except by a force that stops it. Likewise, a body at rest remains at rest until a force comes to move it.

So: force either moves what is at rest, or stills what is moving and checks it. An example of this is what we see on railways, with the buffers that stop the train; for if you want to stop the train, you cut off its fuel, but the thrust that moves it remains and needs an opposing force to stop it. This is what they call the law of inertia. That is: if a thing is moving it needs a force to stop it, and if it is at rest it needs a force to move it.

Among this is the law of inertia (al-qusur al-dhati, "inherent insufficiency") which we were taught in schools. You notice it when a car starts moving and you find your body pushed backwards, because it moved forward while you were at rest; and if the car stops, your body is thrown forward because it stopped while you were moving. So these things that move in the universe, or that are still, are the result of a force.

Thus His saying, Most High: ﴿Take the Book with strength﴾ [19:12], because the Book contains commands and prohibitions: it orders good and forbids you from evil. If it orders you to good while you do not do it, you need a driving force that pushes you to good, as if you were at rest and needed a force to move you. And if it forbids you from evil while you are doing it, you need a force that restrains you and halts your movement into evil. The method is this force that moves you toward good when you are at rest, and stills you from evil when you are in motion.

Then He says, Most High: ﴿And We gave him judgement while still a child﴾ [19:12].

Judgement (al-hukm) means knowledge and understanding of the Torah, or obedience and worship. ﴿While still a child﴾ means at an early age, because the matter is a gift from God that is not subject to causes. Yahya, peace be upon him, came to maturity and intelligence early, surpassing his peers while he was young, so that his peers called him: "Were we not created for play?"

Because Yahya came into the world when his parents were old and weak, he was like a child who needs someone to shower him with tenderness and affection, to make up for the tenderness of his parents, and who needs someone to teach and raise him. Therefore the Truth, glorified and exalted is He, took this task upon Himself. He, glorified is He, is his Creator, the One who named him, and the One who takes charge of him, so He granted him tenderness from Him, glorified is He:

(from Us.. "13" Maryam) from Our side, because the capacity for tenderness in the parents had run dry. And His saying:

﴿and purity.. "13"﴾ (Surat Maryam) meaning purity from sins, purity of soul and blessing. All of these are the result of divine upbringing through the method of God, which charts his movement in life: do this and do not do that.

﴿and he was pious "13"﴾ (Surat Maryam) meaning: he responded to this tenderness. This upbringing bore fruit in him, so he was pious, that is, one who carries out the commands of God and avoids His prohibitions, and by that he shielded himself from the attributes of majesty of God, exalted is He. We have said that taqwa (God-consciousness, piety) is that you place between yourself and what you fear a barrier that protects you and keeps you away from its harm. So you say: "Fear God (ittaqi Allah) and fear the Fire (ittaqi al-nar)." How is that, when we want to reach His companionship, glorified is He?

We say: "Fear God" means: place between yourself and the attributes of His majesty and omnipotence a shield that protects you from His might, His overpowering nature and His subjugation, for you are not able to bear the least of punishment. The Fire is among the soldiers of God and a manifestation of His subjugation, so guarding against the Fire is part of guarding against God. The shield that protects you from the attributes of might and majesty is obedience, by carrying out the commands and avoiding the prohibitions.

Despite the fact that Yahya (peace be upon him) came to his parents when they were elderly and frail, and he did not receive from them sufficient tenderness or appropriate upbringing, and he did not feel complete fatherhood with them, so their role in his life was secondary, and their care for him was faint and modest, nevertheless, with all of this, he was dutiful to them and tender toward them. And He also said about him:

﴿And he was not arrogant, disobedient.﴾ (Surah Maryam 19:14)

The attributes of arrogance (jabarut) and disobedience (ʿisyan) cannot be conceived of in a child toward his parents except when he sees from his father neglect and turning away from his care, and when he sees from his mother preoccupation with his upbringing, for she leaves him without regard for his right.

Therefore we see examples of this arrogance and this disobedience, and we hear of those who are harsh toward their mothers and their fathers, because they did not find from them kindness, tenderness and care, so the bonds of fatherhood between them were severed. It seems that Zakariyya related to his son what had happened and recounted to him his story, so the son understood the role of his parents and negated any shortcoming on their part, so he was dutiful and merciful to them, and humble and obedient to them.

These are three matters that mark the milestones of a human being's life: birth, death, and resurrection. God singled him out for peace on the day of his birth, because he was born in a manner contrary to the usual way of birth: his mother was barren and had reached old age. Yet she was not exposed to the tongues of people, and no one objected to her giving birth while in this state, and so no one dared to speak against her, because what happened to her was a sign (āyah) from the signs of God. God had given Zechariah the good news of it, so that the good news would serve as a preparation and an introduction to this wondrous event.

And He singled him out for peace on the day he dies, because he will die as a martyr (shahīd), and martyrdom is other than death. Martyrdom gives him a life joined to the eternal, everlasting life. And likewise He singled him out on the Day of Resurrection, the day he is raised alive.

The story of Maryam (Mary) in fact came before the story of Zakariyya (Zechariah) and Yahya (John). Zakariyya's request for a son resulted from what he heard from Maryam when he asked her about food he had not brought her, although he was her guardian and the one responsible for her affairs. He was amazed to find with her a provision he had not brought to her, while she was devoted to worship in her sanctuary (mihrab). So he said to her:

﴿O Maryam, from where is this for you?﴾ She said, ﴿It is from Allah. Indeed, Allah provides for whom He wills without account.﴾ (Surah Al ʿImran 3:37)

It is as if this was the first beginning of a principle: "From where is this for you?" But His giving, exalted is He, is not subject to causes. Rather, He, glorified is He, provides for whom He wills, when He wills, and without account. The will of Allah decreed that Maryam utter this statement: ﴿Indeed, Allah provides for whom He wills without account.﴾ (Surah Al ʿImran 3:37) Because it would alert Zakariyya to something, and Maryam herself would also need it later, when she felt pregnant without a husband. She would not object to this situation, and she would know that it was a gift from Allah.

Likewise, this verse alerted Zakariyya, peace be upon him, to the bounty of Allah and the breadth of His mercy. This is a matter that does not escape the Prophet of Allah, but there are concerns in the human soul which, although they are far from the focus of awareness and far from attention, become noticed when they are mentioned. Therefore, the Truth, glorified and exalted is He, says: ﴿There Zakariyya called upon his Lord...﴾ (Surah Al ʿImran 3:38)

So since Allah provides for whom He wills without account, why should I not ask Allah for a righteous son who will carry the mission of the call after me? And since provision is without account, old age, barrenness, or anything else will not prevent it.

Thus, it was Maryam who inspired Zakariyya with this supplication, and Allah answered Zakariyya and granted him Yahya, so that this would be an introduction and preparation for Maryam, so that she would not be disturbed by her pregnancy, and would refer this matter to the fact that Allah provides for whom He wills without account. This was to comfort her soul and reassure her. Otherwise, it would be possible for doubts to play with her and suspicions to afflict her, and she might imagine that this pregnancy was the result of something that happened without her awareness, or that she had been asleep, for example.

But the Truth, blessed and exalted is He, cuts off all these doubts from her, and gives her a precedent that she sees and experiences herself: food that no one had brought to her, and the pregnancy of Zakariyya's wife, who was barren and could not bear children.

The words of the Exalted:

﴿Mention in the Book Maryam...﴾ (Surah Maryam 19:16)

"The Book" is the Noble Qur'an. That is: mention, O Muhammad, in the Book of Allah which He revealed to you, the story of Maryam. The story of this has already been discussed in Surah Al ʿImran, when the Truth, glorified and exalted is He, spoke of the vow of her mother concerning what was in her womb, to serve Bayt al-Maqdis (the Holy House in Jerusalem). Only males, who bear the hardship of this work, were suitable for serving Bayt al-Maqdis. When she gave birth to a female, her expectation did not match the will of Allah. Maryam could not serve the House physically, but she devoted herself to its service in matters of guardianship and religion, forcing herself to it by effort, to the extent that she left her family and went to this place she had chosen as a retreat for worshipping Allah, away from the eyes of people.

Maryam is the daughter of ʿImran, and the Qur'an, in addressing her, said:

﴿O sister of Harun...﴾ (Surah Maryam 19:28)

For this reason, confusion occurred among many people, who thought she was the sister of the Prophet of Allah Musa (Moses) son of ʿImran and the sister of Harun (Aaron), the brother of Musa, peace be upon them both.

The truth is that this matter was a coincidence in which the names agreed. For this reason, when some of the Companions (ṣaḥābah) went to Yemen, its people said to them: "You say that Maryam is the sister of Musa and Harun, although between Maryam and ʿImran, the father of Musa, there are eleven generations!"

The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Did you not mention to them that people used to take omens by naming, especially the Prophets, so they named their children after them: ʿImran, and they named their children after them: Harun."

They even mentioned that at the funeral of one of the scholars, four thousand men named Harun walked in it. So the names here are a coincidence: she is the daughter of ʿImran, but not the father of Musa, and the sister of Harun, but not the brother of Musa.

The Qur'an dedicated an entire surah to the name of Maryam, singled her out and identified her by her name and her father's name. We have already explained that the specification in the story of Maryam came because she was unique and singular among the women of the world, with a matter that does not happen and will never happen except to her. This is a personal matter that will not be repeated in another of the daughters of Hawwa' (Eve).

But if the matter is general and may be repeated, the story comes without specification, as in the Qur'an's account of the wife of Nuh (Noah) and the wife of Lut (Lot) as examples of disbelief, although they were wives of two noble prophets, and of the wife of Fir'awn (Pharaoh) as an example of faith that arose in the house of disbelief and in its very home. The intent here is not the individuals, but to clarify freedom of belief, and that the woman in Islam has independent, self-standing religious freedom, and that she is not subordinate in her belief to anyone, whether she is the wife of a prophet or the wife of a leader of disbelief.

The words of the Exalted:

﴿when she withdrew from her family to a place toward the east﴾ (Surah Maryam 19:16)

﴿withdrew from her family...﴾ (Surah Maryam 19:16)

That is: she distanced herself from them, from "nabadha al-shay'" meaning he removed it and put it far away. It is as if her intimacy was not with her family, but with the Lord of the family. The Qur'an says ﴿from her family...﴾ (Surah Maryam 19:16) and did not say "from the people," for Maryam left the closest people to her and the dearest to her, and went to this place, ﴿a place toward the east﴾ (Surah Maryam 19:16).

But toward the east of what? Every place may be east and may be west, so the word revolves around every place. But there is a prominent landmark in this place, which is Bayt al-Maqdis. So the meaning is: east of Bayt al-Maqdis. Her withdrawal from her family to this holy place came so that she could devote herself to worship and to serving this place.

But why did she choose the eastern side of Bayt al-Maqdis specifically, rather than other directions? They said: because they used to take omens from the rising of the sun, since it is the sign of material light by which people walk guided, so they do not stumble. A person in his journey has two lights: material light from the sun, the moon, the stars and lamps, which shows him the things around him, so he does not collide with what is stronger than him and destroy you, nor with what is weaker and be destroyed by you.

Likewise, he has a light from the method of Allah which guides him in matters of values, so that he does not wander bewildered among their paths. Among this is the saying of the Exalted: ﴿Allah is the Light of the heavens and the earth...﴾ (Surah al-Nur 24:35)

Then He says after it: ﴿Light upon light...﴾ (Surah al-Nur 24:35) That is: the light of the heaven which descends with revelation to guide people.

Al-Hijab: it is the screen that veils a person from others and veils others from him. So what is the benefit of her taking a screen between herself and her family after she had already withdrawn far from them? We say: she withdrew from her family to a far-off place. This refers to place; but it does not preclude that there be another "makin" (one who is established/located) who screens her so that no one sees her. Thus there is a place (makan) and a place-holder (makin).

A hijab may be a single (mufrad) hijab, which is merely a screen, or it may be a hijab screened by the hijab of another, in which case it is a compound (murakkab) hijab, just as the people of the hijab themselves make a screen. Among this is His, the Exalted's, saying:

﴿And when you recite the Qur'an, We place between you and those who do not believe in the Hereafter a hidden barrier﴾ (Surat al-Isra', 45)

And His saying, the Exalted: ﴿So We sent to her Our Spirit...﴾ (Surat Maryam, 17).

The word "ruh" (spirit) in the Noble Qur'an has multiple applications. The first is the spirit by which our material life is sustained: when God breathes the spirit into matter, life, sensation and movement take hold in it, and all the body's systems turn. This meaning is in His saying: ﴿So when I have proportioned him and breathed into him of My spirit, fall down to him in prostration﴾ (Surat al-Hijr, 29).

But is this life that flows into matter by a spirit from God the life intended by God's creation of creatures? They said: if this life were the intended one, how paltry it would be, because a person may pass through it and die after an hour, or a day, or a year, or several years.

So it is a short, base, trivial life, closer to the life of worms and insects. As for man, whom God honoured and for whose sake He created the cosmos, there must be another life suited to God's honouring him. This other life, enduring and everlasting, the Qur'an speaks of, saying:

﴿And indeed, the Last Abode - that is the [true] life, if only they knew﴾ (Surat al-'Ankabut, 64).

(Lahiya al-hayawan) means: the real life. As for your worldly life, it is threatened by death, even if you reach extreme old age ('ataa), for your end is death. If you want the true life that no death threatens, it is in the Hereafter.

If the Creator, blessed and exalted, gave you a spirit in this world by which you move and which suits the duration of your stay in it, will He not give you in the Hereafter a spirit suited to it, suited to its permanence and everlastingness? When the Qur'an speaks of this spirit, it says to people:

﴿O you who have believed, respond to Allah and to the Messenger when he calls you to that which gives you life...﴾ (Surat al-Anfal, 24).

How does He call them to what gives them life, and address them while they are alive? Yes, they are alive with the life of this world, but He calls them to another life, enduring and lasting. As for one who answers this call and strives for this life, he will receive only this short, perishing life that has no permanence.

Just as God named the secret He breathes into matter, so that movement and life stir in it, "ruh" (spirit), so He named the values by which souls live a happy life "ruh", as He said:

﴿And thus We have revealed to you a Spirit of Our command...﴾ (Surat al-Shura, 52)

That is, the Noble Qur'an. And He named the angel who descends with the spirit "ruh":

﴿The Trustworthy Spirit has brought it down﴾ (Surat al-Shu'ara', 193), and he is Jibril, peace be upon him. So His saying, the Exalted: ﴿So We sent to her Our Spirit...﴾ (Surat Maryam, 17) means: Jibril, peace be upon him.

﴿...and he appeared to her as a well-proportioned man﴾ (Surat Maryam, 17). The meaning of "tamaththala" (appeared): this is not his true reality; he presented himself to her in that form, whereas his true reality is luminous, with other attributes, and with wings, two, three, and four. So why then did the angel come to Maryam in human form?

Because the two were going to meet, and this meeting could not take place secretly; likewise it is impossible for an angel to meet humans with his angelic nature, for each has his own law that does not suit the other. In their meeting, the angel must be imagined in the form of a man, or humans must rise to the attributes of the angels, as Muhammad, may God bless him and grant him peace, rose to the attributes of the angels in the event of the Isra' and Mi'raj. The meeting between the two kinds occurs only through this approximation.

Therefore, when the disbelievers asked that the Messenger be an angel, the Truth, blessed and exalted, answered them:

﴿Say, "If there had been upon the earth angels walking secure, We would have sent down to them from the heaven an angel messenger."﴾ (Surat al-Isra', 95). And He said: ﴿And if We had made him an angel, We would have made him a man and would have covered for them what they cover.﴾ (Surat al-An'am, 9).

So: the angel cannot meet humans except through this approximation. Jibril, peace be upon him, came to Maryam in human form so that she would be at ease with him and not be frightened if she saw him in his angelic form. ﴿...appearing to her as a man﴾ (Surat Maryam, 17), that is, of her kind; ﴿well-proportioned﴾ (Surat Maryam, 17), that is, sound in form and make, handsome, his limbs harmonious and well-matched in the most beautiful way a human can be, so that nothing marred him, such as a large forehead, nose, or mouth, as we see in some people.

All of this was to put Maryam at ease and reassure her, and also to establish that she was the chaste virgin; for when she saw this handsome, comely youth, she showed him no admiration, did not speak to him with softness, and uttered not a single word from which any inclination toward him could be understood.

Thus she did not show him any admiration, nor did he address her with a single word, and this is evidence of her chastity, purity, uprightness and steadfastness. Her words:

﴿I seek refuge.. " 18 "﴾ (Surat Maryam)

That is: I take refuge and seek protection with God from you, because I fear that you will harm me or assault me while I am weak, having no power or might except through God, so I seek refuge in Him from you. The believer is one who respects the seeking of refuge in God and honours it: if you seek refuge in God, He will give you refuge, and if you seek protection in God, He will protect you.

When the Prophet (ﷺ) proposed to a woman, and she had some beauty that aroused the jealousy of his wives, they feared that she would overcome them in the heart of the Messenger of God (ﷺ), so they plotted against her a matter that would keep her away from them. They told her, being a naive and unsophisticated young woman, that when the Messenger of God (ﷺ) is approached by a person he likes him to say: "I seek refuge in God from you." So when she entered upon him, the woman did exactly that before the Messenger of God (ﷺ), and he said to her: "You have sought refuge with one who grants refuge; return to your family."

So Maryam's words: ﴿Indeed I seek refuge in the Most Merciful from you, if you are God-fearing﴾ (Surat Maryam, 18) — because the God-fearing believer is one who fears God and respects the seeking of refuge in Him. It is as though she said: if you are God-fearing, then keep away from me. She chose to seek refuge in the Most Merciful because of her hope that, if he were not a believer and God-fearing, he would keep away from her out of mercy for her and her weakness, and she turned to the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate, who would shield and guard her from him.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1–53, fragments of 54–66) on surah 19, verse 19:

He said:

﴿I am only the messenger of your Lord, to announce to you a pure son.﴾ (Surah Maryam 19:19)

He was not the messenger of Allah, because the Lord (al-Rabb) is the one who takes charge of nurturing, who perfects it and protects it from corruption. The gift of lordship is thus a material gift, whereas the gift of divinity (al-uluhiyyah) is a spiritual, moral gift, which is worship. So, "I am the messenger of your Lord, who takes charge of you, cares for you and guards you, so do not fear."

As for His saying, ﴿to bestow upon you...﴾ (Surah Maryam 19:19), it implies that what will happen to Maryam is a gift from Allah not subject to the natural causes (al-asbab al-takwiniyyah). The gift in this case is a true and pure gift, and a real miracle. We have said in the story of Zakariya and Yahya that Allah the Exalted bestowed Yahya upon Zakariya while he was advanced in age and his wife was barren; but in any case both reproductive organs were present, the male and the female. In Maryam's case, however, she is a female without a male, so here is the pure gift and the true miracle.

As for His saying:

﴿a pure boy﴾ (Surah Maryam 19:19), meaning: purified, cleansed, pure in his creation.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 19, verse 20:

(Anná) is an interrogative about the modes by which this matter could come about, and an expression of wonder at how such a thing could happen. And His saying:

﴿Has touched me...﴾ (20) (Surah Maryam):

"Touch" (mass) here is a metaphor and a polite expression for marriage (nikah). Maryam denied every form of union between a male and a female when she said:

﴿No man has touched me, and I have not been unchaste.﴾ (20) (Surah Maryam).

The meeting of a male with a female has means. The first means: lawful marriage, which Allah prescribed for His servants for procreation and the preservation of lineage. It consists of offer and acceptance, a contract, and witnessing; this is the lawful touch.

The second means: that this meeting take place in a forbidden manner, with the woman's consent or by force against her. Maryam denied herself all of these means, saying:

﴿No man has touched me...﴾ (Surah Maryam)

neither in what is lawful nor in what is unlawful, and I myself am

﴿not unchaste﴾ (Surah Maryam).

So then: from where would I have a boy?

The word "mass" (massa) has come in the Qur'an to denote sexual intercourse, as in His saying, Exalted is He:

﴿There is no blame upon you if you divorce women before you have touched them...﴾ (236) (Surah al-Baqarah).

So the intended meaning of "touch" here is intercourse. For this reason Imam Abu Hanifa interpreted His saying, Exalted is He:

﴿Or you have touched women...﴾ (43) (Surah al-Ma'idah/al-Nisa')

as meaning intercourse, because the Qur'an used "touch" and intended by it marriage. Touching (massa) is an act from one side only, whereas mulamasah (lamasa) is a reciprocal action between two parties, so it is by a fortiori meaning: you have had intercourse. And her saying:

﴿and I have not been unchaste﴾ (20) (Surah Maryam).

Al-baghy: is the woman who solicits men. Al-bigha'/baghaa': is fornication (zina), and al-baghiy: is she who offers herself to men and invites them, and perhaps forces them into this crime. And her saying:

﴿unchaste﴾ (20) (Surah Maryam)

is an intensive form of "al-baghy," which is wrongdoing (zulm). She chose the intensive form baghiy and did not say baghiyah (active participle), because baghiyah relates to rights concerning what is around the honour, whereas assault upon the honour itself suits the intensive form of this act.

Just as the Truth, glory be to Him, said to Zakariyya when he marvelled that he should have a son:

﴿He said: "Thus (it is). Your Lord says..."﴾ (Surah Maryam)

That is: I know what you are in of old age, and that your wife is barren and cannot bear. But the matter has come from Allah and His judgment has been issued, and He alone possesses execution. So why the wonder then?

Here some of those who harbour doubts about the Qur'an object to His saying, "Kadhalika" (thus) with a fatha in the story of Zakariyya and with a kasra in the story of Maryam ("kadhaliki"), while the context and meaning are one. Which of the two is more eloquent than the other? And if one of them is eloquent, is the other not eloquent?

This objection of theirs results from the shortcoming of their understanding of the words of Allah. The word "kadhalika" is composed of "dha", a demonstrative noun, and the kaf of address, which takes a fatha when addressing a masculine and a kasra when addressing a feminine.

Here too He said, "Your Lord" — that is, the One who takes charge of your upbringing and care, and whom his Lord raises with complete upbringing that enables him to carry out the task intended for the one being raised. And His saying:

﴿"It is easy for Me..." 21﴾ (Surah Maryam)

As He said regarding the matter of resurrection after death:

﴿"And it is easier for Him..." 27﴾ (Surah al-Rum). The words "hayyin" (easy) and "ahwan" (easier), with respect to the Truth, blessed and exalted, are not to be taken in their literal sense, because "hayyin" and "ahwan" imply "sa'b" (difficult) and "a'sab" (more difficult). These are matters that suit human action in dealing with things according to his capacity and resources. As for the Creator, glory be to Him, there is nothing easy or easier for Him than another, because He, glory be to Him, does not perform actions by treatment or practice, but by His saying "Be" (kun). So the Truth, glory be to Him, addresses us according to the measure of our minds. Thus His saying:

﴿"It is easy for Me..." 21﴾ (Surah Maryam) means: by your own reckoning, if I created you from nothing, then restoring you from something existing is an easy matter.

Then He, exalted is He, says:

﴿"And that We may make him a sign for mankind and a mercy from Us..." 21﴾ (Surah Maryam)

Was the purpose of creating Jesus, peace be upon him, in this form only that the Truth, glory be to Him, should display His power in creation and the absoluteness of His power? No, rather there is another purpose: ﴿"that We may make him a sign for mankind..." 21﴾ (Surah Maryam), that is, a wondrous matter that goes beyond customary habit and causes. As we say: "this is a sign in beauty, a sign in intelligence," for "ayah" is only said of a thing that departs from what is commonly encountered.

The sign here is that the Creator, blessed and exalted, created Adam, peace be upon him, without a father or mother, and created Hawwa' without a mother, and created Jesus, peace be upon him, from a mother without a father; then He creates all of you from a father and a mother, and sometimes a father and mother exist yet Allah does not will for them, so He makes whom He wills barren.

So this is a matter governed only by the will of the One who brings into being, glory be to Him. The sign is for people to know the absoluteness of His power in creation, and that it is not subject to causes, and that it is not a mechanical process, but a will of the Creator, glory be to Him, to will or not to will.

But was the sign in the creation of Jesus, peace be upon him, or in his mother? It was possible for Jesus to exist from a father and mother; so the sign is in his mother, and she is the original cause of this sign. Therefore He, exalted is He, says in another verse:

﴿"And We made the son of Maryam and his mother a sign..." 50﴾ (Surah al-Mu'minun).

So Jesus and Maryam are one sign, not two, because they are not separable. Then He, exalted is He, says:

﴿"...and a mercy from Us." 21﴾ (Surah Maryam).

The aspect of mercy in creating Jesus, peace be upon him, in this form is that He, glory be to Him, spares people from doubting that the power of Allah is bound to and dependent on causes. Even if this doubt is merely a passing thought, it is neither permissible nor valid with respect to the Creator, glory be to Him. It is as if He, blessed and exalted, is sparing us from mere passing thoughts by a reality that confirms that absolute power brings creation from something, from part of something, and from nothing.

His saying: ﴿"And it was a matter decreed." 21﴾ (Surah Maryam) means: a settled matter that admits no dispute, so beware of disputing about its modality. For speech about a future thing, if it comes from a speaker who does not possess the power to execute what he says, then his intention may not be fulfilled for any reason. For example, you say, "I will do such-and-such tomorrow," and tomorrow comes and many things, perhaps beyond your control, come between you and what you want. Thus you do not possess all the elements of the action.

But when the speech is from Allah, who possesses all the elements of the action, His word is true and actual. So He, exalted is He, says:

﴿"And it was a matter decreed." 21﴾ (Surah Maryam).

When we spoke about the divisions of verbs into the past, which occurred before the speech, and the present, which occurs now or in the future, we said that these tenses, with respect to the Truth, glory be to Him, are dissolved of pastness, presentness and futurity.

So when He, exalted is He, says: ﴿"And Allah has always been Forgiving, Merciful." 14﴾ (Surah al-Fath).

Was the Truth, glory be to Him, forgiving and merciful in the past, and not so in the present and future? No, because the Truth, glory be to Him, was and still is Forgiving and Merciful; His mercy and forgiveness are eternal, even before there existed anyone to be forgiven or shown mercy.

Therefore the verb came in the past form, for the attribute exists in Him, glory be to Him, from eternity. He, glory be to Him, is a Creator before He created creation, and He created by the attribute of creating. As we gave an example for this: we say, "So-and-so is a poet." Is he a poet because he composed a qasida? Or did he compose the qasida because he is a poet, and by poetry he made the qasida? Thus he is a poet before he composed the qasida, and had the attribute not been in him, he would not have composed it.

So the attribute is eternal in the Truth, glory be to Him. When you say, ﴿"And Allah has always been Forgiving, Merciful." 14﴾ (Surah al-Fath), this attribute has been established for Him from eternity, and because He, glory be to Him, does not change, and no one opposes Him, it has remained for Him. This is the meaning of "He was and still is." This matter is clear in the opening of Surah al-Nahl:

﴿"The command of Allah has come, so do not seek to hasten it." 1﴾ (Surah al-Nahl).

For this reason some orientalists paused before this verse: how does He, glory be to Him, say "has come" in the past form and then say "so do not seek to hasten it," that is, in the future? We say: because His saying "has come" is a settled matter about which there is no doubt or dispute; there is no other power opposing it or preventing its occurrence. Therefore it came in the past form, though in reality it is a future matter.

(So she carried him) — that is, she carried him, with the verb's object elided and the preposition connected: the verb "carry" (ḥamala) requires a carrier and something carried.

﴿So she withdrew with him to a remote place﴾ (Surah Maryam, 19:22). Do not think that this incident in the story is a repeated one. The first withdrawal (intibādh) was for seclusion for worship, whereas here ﴿she withdrew with him﴾ (Surah Maryam, 19:22) means that she moved away from her people when she sensed the pregnancy, and she feared people's eyes and their curiosity, so she went out to a distant place.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 19, verse 23:

﴿So the pains of childbirth drove her﴾ (Surah Maryam).

The verb jā'a fulān means that he came of his own choice and will. Ajā'ahu fulān means that he brought him against his will and without his intention. It is as if the labour pains were what compelled her to the trunk of the palm tree and forced her to go to this place against her will.

﴿So the pains of childbirth drove her﴾ (Surah Maryam), i.e. he brought her, as if there were a force outside her pulling her to this place. Al-makhāḍ (the pain of labour) is the pain that overtakes a woman before delivery, and it is not the ṭalq (the early contractions that precede the descent of the fetus). His saying: ﴿So the pains of childbirth drove her to the trunk of the palm tree﴾ (Surah Maryam).
